name: Why a sharp knife is safer than a dull one
scope: The counterintuitive truth: the sharp knife is the safe one. T1: a sharp knife is SAFER than a dull one because it bites where you aim, needs far less force, and is far less likely to slip. T2: the edge is a thin WEDGE — a sharp apex concentrates your push onto a tiny line of contact so it parts food with little pressure, while a dull edge spreads the force and just squashes. T3: why a dull knife SKATES off a tomato's or onion's taut skin instead of biting — it slides, and a slide toward your hand is how cooks get cut. T4: the trade-off built into the edge ANGLE — a narrower bevel is keener but chips, a wider bevel is duller but tougher (why a chopping cleaver's edge is stouter than a slicer's). T5: 'toothy' vs 'polished' micro-edge — a coarse-stone edge has microscopic teeth that grab tomato skin, while a polished edge glides for clean push-cuts on fish, so you match the edge finish to the food.
source: Culinary knife-safety references; Japanese Knife Lab sharpening-angle guide (bevel geometry); Serious Eats / Cook's Illustrated knife-physics writeups.
framing_note: Answer is always a concrete edge-physics or food fact (bites vs skates, wedge concentrates force, angle trade-off, toothy vs polished), never a bare 'safety tip'. Lead with the scene ('your knife skids off the tomato skin toward your thumb'), never 'What is a sharp edge?'. Accuracy rail: sharp-is-safer is about FORCE + PREDICTABILITY (less push, no skate, cuts where aimed), NOT the myth that a dull knife can't cut you. Dinner-test payoff: T3, the skate-off-the-tomato rung.

name: Sharpening vs. honing — grinding a new edge vs. straightening the old one
scope: Two different jobs cooks constantly confuse. T1: a honing steel does NOT sharpen — it straightens; everyday cutting rolls the thin edge over sideways, and a few strokes on the steel realign it so it feels sharp again. T2: a whetstone (a sharpening STONE) actually SHARPENS by grinding away metal to form a brand-new apex — you do this occasionally, honing you do often. T3: the whetstone GRIT ladder — a coarse stone removes metal fast to set the edge, a fine stone polishes it, and you climb from low grit to high like sandpaper. T4: the BURR — sharpening raises a tiny wire of bent metal on the far side that tells you the two bevels have finally met; you flip and grind the other side, then remove it. T5: STROPPING — dragging the edge backward on leather wipes off the last burr and micro-scratches, taking the blade from sharp to scary-sharp while removing almost no real metal.
source: Knives and Tools (honing vs sharpening steel); Borough Kitchen whetstone/steel guide; Chef's Vision stropping-vs-honing; Japanese Knife Lab.
framing_note: Each answer names the correct TOOL and its mechanism (steel realigns, stone removes metal, coarse-then-fine, the burr, the strop). Anti-restatement: the stem must not give away 'removes metal vs realigns' — the player must KNOW which tool does which, all four choices live. Accuracy rail: honing removes essentially no metal, it bends the rolled edge back — it is NOT a mild sharpening. Payoff: T1, the 'honing isn't sharpening' reveal (the most common kitchen myth).

name: Anatomy of a chef's knife — every part has a job
scope: A chef's knife is a whole tool kit in one blade. T1: the TIP (point) is for fine, precise work — scoring, trimming, small controlled cuts, piercing. T2: the HEEL (the back of the edge, nearest the handle) is for FORCE — the strongest part of the edge, where you drive down through a hard carrot or winter squash. T3: the BELLY (the curved section of the edge) is what lets a knife ROCK — a curved belly rocks, a dead-flat one can't. T4: the BOLSTER (the thick collar where blade meets handle) adds balance AND acts as a finger guard so a wet hand can't slide forward onto the edge. T5: the TANG — the steel that runs back inside the handle; a FULL tang runs the whole length for balance and strength, which is why a good knife feels planted rather than tip-heavy. (Context: the SPINE is the blunt back — you press on it or crush a garlic clove with the flat.)
source: Shun Cutlery knife-anatomy; The Kitchn 'anatomy of a chef's knife'; Misen knife-anatomy guide; Element Knife Company.
framing_note: Every answer names a PART and the JOB it does (tip=precision, heel=force, belly=rocking, bolster=guard+balance, tang=balance/strength). Scene-led ('you need to power through the dense neck of a butternut squash — which part of the blade do you drive down with?'), never 'What is the heel?'. Accuracy rail: the bolster's finger-guard role is real but NOT every knife has a full bolster (many Japanese knives skip it) — phrase as 'on knives that have one.' Payoff: T4, the bolster-as-finger-guard (its real reason for existing is a surprise).

name: The basic cuts — chop, slice, dice, mince
scope: The everyday four, and why size is the whole point. T1: to DICE is to cut into even CUBES — the game is evenness so every piece cooks at the same rate. T2: to MINCE is to cut as FINE as possible (garlic, ginger) so the flavor spreads through the whole dish and can nearly melt away. T3: CHOP vs SLICE — chopping makes rough, roughly-even pieces where precision doesn't matter; slicing makes flat, even planks with a drawing motion. T4: why UNEVEN cuts wreck a dish — in one hot pan the small bits scorch while the big bits stay raw; a loose 'rough chop' is fine for a long-simmered stock but wrong for a quick sauté. T5: dicing done right goes PLANK then STICK then cube — you cut a flat slab, cut that into batons, then crosscut the batons; even pros build a dice in that order.
source: Rouxbe 'types of knife cuts'; Wikipedia 'List of culinary knife cuts'; Wekiva Culinary basic-cuts guide.
framing_note: Answer is the specific cut/technique or the cooking consequence (even cuts = even cooking). Anti-restatement: the 'why even' rungs must not state the reason in the stem. Accuracy rail: mince = finest/irregular (great for garlic) — do NOT conflate it with brunoise, which is a precise geometric cube owned by the French-cuts ladder. Payoff: T4, the scorch-vs-raw-in-one-pan rung (the reason evenness matters).

name: The French precision cuts — julienne, brunoise, batonnet, chiffonade
scope: The classical cuts, defined by exact SHAPE and how they nest inside one another. T1: JULIENNE is the matchstick — long, thin, square-sided sticks (shoestring), the cut behind a pile of matchstick carrots. T2: BATONNET is the julienne's big brother, a thicker square stick — it is literally the shape of a classic French fry. T3: BRUNOISE is a tiny cube made BY crosscutting a julienne — you julienne first, then chop across, so brunoise is a julienne turned into confetti. T4: CHIFFONADE isn't a stick at all — you stack leaves (basil, mint), roll them like a cigar, and slice to get fine RIBBONS. T5: why classical cuts obsess over identical size — a brunoise garnish must cook and look uniform; it's the SAME even-cooking logic pushed to precision (and the tourné, a hand-carved 7-sided 'football,' exists purely so every piece cooks and plates identically).
source: Wikipedia 'List of culinary knife cuts' (with dimensions); Rouxbe knife-cuts; Snippets of Paris 'French knife cuts'; Wekiva Culinary.
framing_note: Answer names the CUT or its defining relationship (batonnet = fry shape, brunoise = julienne crosscut, chiffonade = rolled ribbons). Exact sizes (1/8 in julienne, 1/4 in batonnet, 7-sided tourné) are CONTEXT/distractors ONLY, never the tested answer (banned exact-number minutiae). Scene-led with the food ('a chef stacks basil leaves, rolls them into a cigar, and slices — what's the cut called?'). Accuracy rail: brunoise is DERIVED from julienne (a cube = a stick crosscut) — keep that nesting relationship correct. Payoff: T3, the 'brunoise is julienne turned to confetti' reveal.

name: Safe hands — the claw, the pinch, and the knife you never catch
scope: The handful of habits that keep fingers attached. T1: the CLAW grip — you curl the fingertips of your guiding hand under and let your KNUCKLES ride against the blade's flat, so the edge physically cannot reach your fingertips. T2: you cut AWAY from your hand and body, never toward the palm, so a slip carries the edge into the board instead of into you. T3: you NEVER try to catch a falling knife — you step back and let it hit the floor, because grabbing closes your hand around a moving edge. T4: the PINCH grip on the handle — thumb and forefinger pinch the blade just ahead of the handle (not a fist gripping the back), which is what gives real control and kills the wobble. T5: you anchor the board with a damp towel underneath and keep the top DRY — a sliding board or a slick, wet tomato is exactly how the blade jumps.
source: Culinary-school and ServSafe knife-safety basics; Rouxbe technique guides; standard professional-kitchen safety doctrine.
framing_note: Answer is a concrete technique plus the reason it works (claw = knuckles guide the blade, pinch = control, step back = don't grab a moving edge, damp towel = board can't slide). Scene-led ('your knife slides off the counter edge toward your foot — what do you do?'). This is cooking TECHNIQUE, which counts as food-anchored. Accuracy rail: 'never catch a falling knife' is universal kitchen doctrine — state it plainly, no hedging. Payoff: T3, the falling-knife rule (the vivid, memorable one).

name: Rocking vs. push-cutting — the blade shape decides the motion
scope: The cut you use is written into the blade's curve. T1: the ROCK cut — you keep the tip planted on the board and rock the curved belly down through herbs and garlic, mincing fast without ever lifting the knife off the board. T2: the PUSH cut (and its pull-cut cousin) — a straighter blade goes straight down and forward in one clean stroke; there's no belly to rock on. T3: why shape MATCHES motion — a French/German chef's knife has a pronounced curved belly built for rocking, while a Japanese santoku or nakiri is much FLATTER, built to push-cut straight down. T4: the Chinese CLEAVER (cai dao) — a broad rectangle that chops straight down and then SCOOPS the whole pile up on its wide face to carry to the wok. T5: why sticky foods cling to the blade — push-cutting straight through leaves potato slices stuck flat to the steel by suction, which is why some blades wear dimples (a Granton edge) to break that suction.
source: Japanese Knife Lab blade-profile guides; santoku/nakiri/gyuto knife-type references; culinary technique guides on rocking vs push cutting.
framing_note: Answer is the motion, the matching blade, or the mechanism (rock = curved belly, push = flatter edge, cleaver scoops, Granton dimples break suction). Accuracy rail: santoku/nakiri are flatter and favor push/pull, but don't claim Japanese knives can't rock at all (a gyuto has some belly) — frame as 'flatter, built for push-cutting.' Payoff: T4, the cleaver scoop-and-carry image (or T5's Granton-dimple reveal for the older tier).

name: The steel in the blade — wootz, Damascus, and the hardness trade-off
scope: Where a blade's steel comes from and what it lets the knife do. T1: DAMASCUS blades are famous for a rippling, watery PATTERN running through the metal — the swirls are the steel itself, not paint or an etched-on decoration. T2: the original 'Damascus' swords were forged from WOOTZ, a high-carbon crucible steel first made in INDIA and carried west — European smiths spent centuries unable to copy it. T3: the pattern is a MAP of the steel — networks of hard iron-carbide particles line up into bands during forging, and those bands are the ripple you see. T4: the HARD-vs-TOUGH trade-off in a kitchen knife — a harder blade (Japanese steel) takes a keener edge and holds it longer but is more brittle and can CHIP, while a softer blade (German steel) dulls sooner but shrugs off abuse. T5: CARBON vs STAINLESS — a plain-carbon blade gets sharper and grows a living dark 'patina,' but rusts if left wet, while stainless trades a little keenness to resist rust (why a carbon knife gets wiped dry, never left in the sink).
source: Wikipedia 'Wootz steel' and 'Damascus steel'; Verhoeven & Pendray (TMS/JOM) on trace-element carbide banding and the 'lost' technique; Japanese Knife Lab HRC hardness guide.
framing_note: Every answer is about the BLADE/steel (the pattern IS the metal, wootz = Indian origin, carbide banding, hard-vs-tough, carbon-vs-stainless). Accuracy rails: wootz originated in INDIA / South Asia and was exported TO Damascus — do not call it Syrian/Damascene steel; treat the 'lost recipe' as real but explained (Verhoeven tied it to specific ore's trace elements like vanadium), not as magic. Banned minutiae: never test exact HRC numbers or '1-2% carbon' — those are context; test the CONCEPT (harder = keener but chips). Payoff: T2, the wootz-came-from-India reveal; T4 is the practical dinner-test (why a hard Japanese blade chips).

name: Japanese blades — the single-bevel edge and the one-stroke sashimi cut
scope: A different knife tradition, built around specific foods. T1: the SANTOKU — Japan's everyday all-purpose knife; its name means roughly 'three virtues' because one blade handles meat, fish, and vegetables. T2: the SINGLE bevel — many traditional Japanese knives are sharpened on ONE side only (flat on the back), giving an astonishingly keen edge that cuts paper-thin. T3: the YANAGIBA (the sashimi knife) — long and single-beveled so a slice of raw fish comes off in ONE smooth pull-stroke; sawing back and forth would crush the flesh and dull its shine. T4: the DEBA — a thick, heavy single-bevel knife built to break down a whole fish, riding along the spine and through small bones. T5: why a single bevel STEERS sideways in the food (it naturally curves the cut — great for peeling a sheet-thin ribbon of daikon) and why a right-handed single-bevel knife won't work in a left hand.
source: Japanese Knife Lab knife-types guide; Hasu-Seizo Japanese-knife-types; JIKKO yanagiba reference; santoku/nakiri/deba/usuba sources.
framing_note: Answer is the knife plus the food job it's built for (santoku = all-purpose, yanagiba = one-stroke sashimi, deba = whole fish, single-bevel = keen/steers). Accuracy rails: 'three virtues' — give the common meat/fish/vegetable gloss but note the point is all-purpose; the yanagiba's single pull-stroke genuinely preserves the cut face of raw fish (the real reason sushi chefs use it). Payoff: T3, the one-stroke sashimi cut (the standout wonder).

name: The cutting board — wood, plastic, and the bacteria surprise
scope: The board is a food-safety tool, not just a surface. T1: you keep RAW MEAT and ready-to-eat food (salad, bread) on SEPARATE boards, or wash between, because juices from raw chicken carry the bugs that cause food poisoning. T2: the counterintuitive finding — WOOD boards aren't the germ traps people feared; bacteria left on wood get drawn down into the grain and DIE OFF as the board dries, rather than multiplying. T3: why old PLASTIC can be worse — a knife carves shallow grooves that hold bacteria right at the surface where your next food lands (UC Davis found wood-board users had less foodborne illness). T4: END-GRAIN vs edge-grain — an end-grain board (wood fibers standing up like a bundle of straws) lets the edge slip between fibers, so it's kinder to the knife AND 'self-heals' its cut marks. T5: why you never soak or dishwasher a wood board — waterlogged wood swells and cracks; you wash and dry it fast and oil it, which keeps the surface sealed.
source: Dean O. Cliver / UC Davis Food Safety Lab cutting-board research (naturalhandyman reprint; PubMed Salmonella cross-contamination study); butcherblock.com wood-vs-plastic; end-grain board references.
framing_note: Answer is a board fact plus the food-safety mechanism (separate boards, wood kills bacteria as it dries, plastic grooves harbor bugs, end-grain self-heals). This is an HONEST food-safety truth — present the wood finding as the studied UC-Davis (Cliver) result it is, not folk wisdom. Accuracy rail: don't overclaim wood is 'sterile' — bacteria persist but don't multiply and die off, and separate-boards + washing are still required. Payoff: T2, the wood-kills-bacteria surprise (it defies the intuition that porous wood must be dirtier).

name: Why chopping onions makes you cry — and how a sharp knife helps
scope: A chemical defense the onion never meant for you. T1: an onion isn't 'spicy' — cutting it releases a GAS that drifts up and stings your eyes, and the tears are your eyes flushing away an irritant. T2: the trigger is DAMAGE — an intact onion does nothing; only when you rupture the cells do two things the onion kept apart mix and react to make the eye-stinging compound. T3: why a SHARP knife makes you cry LESS — a keen blade slices cleanly and ruptures fewer cells, so less gas is released, while a dull blade crushes cells and floods the air. T4: why CHILLING the onion first helps — cold slows the reaction that makes the irritant, so a fridge-cold onion gives off the gas more slowly. T5: the irritant becomes a mild ACID the instant it meets the moisture on your eye — that's the chemical sting, and it comes from the onion's SULFUR, the same family that gives garlic its punch.
source: Chemistry World / RSC Education on propanethial-S-oxide (the lachrymatory factor); Bristol 'Molecule of the Month'; Wikipedia 'syn-Propanethial-S-oxide'; Food Republic sharp-knife tip.
framing_note: Answer is the mechanism in plain words (a released gas, damage-triggered, sharp knife = fewer ruptured cells, cold slows it, a mild acid on the eye). Banned minutiae: the enzyme names (alliinase, lachrymatory-factor synthase) and the compound name (syn-propanethial-S-oxide) are CONTEXT/distractors ONLY, never the tested answer. Scene-led ('you're crying over the cutting board — switching to which knife would cut the tears?'). Payoff: T3, the sharp-knife-fewer-tears rung (immediately usable at dinner).

name: The bias cut — why stir-fry veg go on the diagonal
scope: A slanted cut that changes how food cooks. T1: the BIAS cut is a diagonal slice straight across a carrot or scallion instead of a square crosscut. T2: why chefs do it — the slant exposes MORE surface on each piece, so it cooks faster and more evenly in the fast heat of a stir-fry. T3: the ROLL cut (oblique) — you slice on the bias, ROLL the carrot a quarter-turn, and slice again, making chunky wedges that are all surface, ideal for braises and stir-fries.
source: Wikipedia 'List of culinary knife cuts' (oblique/roll cut); stir-fry technique guides.
framing_note: Answer is the cut or the reason it works (diagonal = more exposed surface = faster, more even cooking; roll-cut = all-surface chunks). Accuracy rail: keep the physics honest — more exposed surface area = faster heat transfer. Payoff: T3, the roll-cut reveal (turning one carrot into chunks that are nothing but surface).

name: The serrated knife — teeth that saw bread and bite a tomato
scope: Why the toothy blade beats the smooth one on certain foods. T1: a bread knife has TEETH (serrations) because it SAWS through a crusty loaf — a smooth blade would crush the soft crumb flat before it ever cut the hard crust. T2: on a soft TOMATO, the pointed teeth bite through the taut, slippery skin that a dull straight blade just skids across and squashes. T3: how the teeth work — each point concentrates force to pierce, and the scalloped curves between the points do the cutting as you draw the blade back and forth, needing almost no downward push. T4: why a serrated edge stays 'sharp' for years yet is a pain to fix — the food rides on the tooth TIPS (which wear slowly), and each little scalloped gullet has to be sharpened one at a time, not flat on a stone.
source: Ignited Cutlery 'serrated vs straight'; Kyoku on why serrated knives have teeth; serrated-edge mechanism references.
framing_note: Answer is the mechanism or the matching food (saws the crust without crushing the crumb, teeth bite tomato skin, points pierce while scallops cut, tips wear slowly). Accuracy rail: keep the crush-vs-cut logic right — the serrations let you cut with a sawing draw and very little downward force. Payoff: T2, the tomato-skin bite (the everyday 'aha' every kid has felt).

name: Why cut basil turns black — the case for one clean slice
scope: The bruise you can see. T1: cut or bruised basil turns BLACK/brown within hours — the damaged leaf reacts with the air, the same browning you see on a cut apple. T2: a DULL knife or rough chopping crushes more cells and blackens basil FASTER, while one clean slice with a sharp blade (a chiffonade) keeps it green far longer. T3: why cooks OIL the leaves before slicing (or add a squeeze of lemon) — a coat of oil blocks the air and the acid slows the browning reaction, so the basil stays bright.
source: CalItalia Food and Cookist on basil oxidation; polyphenol-oxidase browning references; chiffonade technique guides.
framing_note: Answer is the mechanism/technique in plain words (air-browning, dull knife crushes more cells, oil blocks the air). Banned minutiae: the enzyme name (polyphenol oxidase / PPO) is CONTEXT only, never the tested answer. This complements the chiffonade SHAPE rung in the French-cuts ladder — here the payoff is the WHY (bruising and oxidation), not the shape. Payoff: T2, the dull-knife-blackens-basil-faster rung (a concrete reason to keep a knife sharp).
